description: SonuX transforms earth observation data into an immersive sensory experience allowing people to hear, see and understand the living rhythms of our planet.
summary:
SonuXBox is an application that  transforms NASA's EIC visualizations into sound, improving accessibility and connecting more people with Earth in a more intuitive, emotional and memorable way.
The current visualizations available at the Earth Information Center (EIC) allow visitors to see how our planet is changing over the years, but this excludes people with visual impairments. Our project takes those visualizations and converts them to audios that are more accessible for people with visual impairments, more engaging and memorable, aiming to reimagine how we experience earth data.
The first working version of SonuxBox is a software application but in future versions the synthesizing engine will be ported to a handheld embedded device that can capture and convert images to songs in real time to enable visually impaired people to easily carry them along to an EIC center to experience the visualizations with their loved ones.
details:
What It Does

SonuxBox is a synthesizer built using C++ to convert NASA's Earth visualizations to sound. C++ was chosen to make it easy to port to a handheld embedded device to increase accessibility.

How It Works

The image is divided into 32 columns and the columns are scanned from left to right. It uses two different modes a terrain mode and an adaptive mode to analyze input images and translate the analysis to musical notes.

The terrain mode identifies specified terrain types across the images. It works better on a natural coloured map of earth. That information is applied to hand written musical rules like; if the vegetation if more than the land the major scale is used, else the minor scale is used of the higher placed land terrains produce a higher pitch in the melody.

The adaptive mode on the other hand makes use of k-means clustering to group pixels of similar colour into 4 groups, assigns the group with the largest number of pixels as the background and makes all the other three groups the signal. The signal is how different a pixel is from the background. The strength of a signal is the average signal in each column of the image and a stronger signal produces a louder note. The height of the signal determines the pitch and the hue determines the key.

The image analysis are then converted to music notes and written to a wave file that is sent to the front-end of the application.

Benefit

The synthesizing engine was built entirely in C++ which would make it easy to build a small handheld based on our CAD design to improve portability and accessibility of the solution. Anyone can easily carry the device along to visit one of the visualization centers to also experience NASA's information. Even though the system was built specifically for NASA's data it can also be used to convert any image to sound using the adaptive mode.

Impact
This project aims to bridge the gap for visually impaired people not only for experiencing NASA's visualizations but connecting them with the world around us.

Tools

C++ was used to build the backend of the application using libraries such as OpenCV, miniaudio and httplib and the frontend was built using. React.js. Super Intelligence was used to aid in the development of the codebase to bridge the knowledge gap in music theory and building web backends using c++.

Creativity

  • The music generated by the synthesizer engine has a retro game-like vibe.
  • The proposed SonuxBox device allows users to hear either an Adaptive audio or a Terrain audio by pressing on either buttons on the device.
  • The notes being played or heard can be seen as well and translated to actual musical readings.

Factors
The team considered accessibility to the visually impaired as the main theme of this project focusing more on how they will be helped by the solution and their user experience.
